analysis.one_liner: Restricts warrantless spying on Americans' international communications under FISA.
analysis.headline: The privacy bill died in committee: introduced with 3 Senate sponsors in August 2012 and referred to the Judiciary Committee, it never received a hearing or vote before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the 2008 FISA amendments (Section 702) so the government cannot deliberately collect an American's communications without a warrant, except in narrow terrorism or imminent-harm cases. It would bar the use in court of information gathered through procedures the secret surveillance court finds deficient, force communications to or from people in the U.S. to be quarantined unless a warrant is obtained within 7 days, and require annual audits by the Justice and Defense Department inspectors general.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans whose phone calls, emails, and other international communications are swept up under FISA Section 702, which currently allows collection targeting foreigners without individual warrants even when the communication involves a person in the United States.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Americans whose communications get swept into surveillance

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits 'reverse targeting': the government could no longer target a person overseas when a significant purpose is actually to acquire the communications of a particular, known person in the United States without going through the warrant process of FISA title I.

Bars communications from being acquired under FISA title VII if the government knows at the time they are to or from someone reasonably believed to be in the United States, with exceptions only for international terrorism directed at the U.S., agent-of-a-foreign-power cases with probable cause, or preventing death or serious bodily harm.

Quarantines any communication to or from a person in the U.S. so no one may access or search it except under a title I warrant; emergency access is limited to 7 days and requires notice to the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court, and information accessed without required notice cannot be used against a U.S. person in any proceeding.

Blocks information obtained through acquisition procedures the FISA court finds deficient (or inconsistent with the Fourth Amendment) from being used in evidence against anyone in the United States or disclosed without consent, unless the government corrects the deficiency and the court approves.
Requires annual audits of compliance by the Defense Department and Justice Department inspectors general, with reports to the Intelligence and Judiciary Committees of both chambers.

analysis.who_pays: Intelligence agencies would lose the ability to freely collect and use communications involving people in the United States without individual warrants, and investigations would face additional court oversight, quarantine rules, and audit requirements.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not ban warrantless acquisition outright: it leaves exceptions for international terrorism directed at the United States, suspected foreign-power agents with probable cause, and imminent death or serious bodily harm, and allows up to 7 days of emergency access before a warrant application, so a substantial amount of collection involving Americans could continue.
Its main protections only take effect once the FISA court approves new government procedures or, at the latest, one year after enactment, so the restrictions would not apply immediately.

Government and intelligence-community defenders argue that collecting foreign communications without individual warrants is essential to counterterrorism and that courts have treated foreigners' overseas communications differently from Americans'; the bill would impose new friction, delay, and evidentiary exclusions on those operations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary Americans the benefit is real: their communications currently can be collected and used with no individual warrant under Section 702, and the bill would add warrant requirements, quarantine rules, evidence limits, and audits. The cost falls mainly on intelligence agencies, which would face more court oversight and narrower collection, though the bill's own terrorism and emergency exceptions leave significant room for continued surveillance. The design is reasonable but incremental: it tightens Section 702 rather than replacing it, and its protections phase in over months.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in early August 2012, read twice, and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which took no further action before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Merkley introduced the Protect America's Privacy Act of 2012 on August 2, 2012, joined by Senators Ron Wyden and Jon Tester.

The bill's only actions were introduction and referral: it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day, and the action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote afterward.
The 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, so the bill died in committee without ever receiving a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Intelligence agencies kept the broad Section 702 collection authority and warrantless access to Americans' international communications that the bill would have restricted, and no member had to take a recorded vote on it.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to add warrant and Fourth Amendment protections for Americans' communications under FISA Section 702.

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as an original co-sponsor at introduction.

for.name: Sen. Jon Tester
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as an original co-sponsor at introduction.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on August 2, 2012 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or committee vote is recorded before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Democrats, but no one voted for or against the bill and no committee or floor vote ever occurred, so the partisan shape of any real opposition is not recorded.

industries.industry: U.S. intelligence agencies (NSA, FBI, and Justice Department surveillance programs)
industries.note: The bill would strip their authority to collect and use communications to or from people in the United States without individual warrants under FISA Section 702, and add audits and evidence exclusions. Their institutional interest in unrestricted collection runs against the privacy interest of ordinary Americans.

industries.industry: Telecommunications and internet companies assisting surveillance
industries.note: The bill does not directly regulate carriers, but tighter rules on what agencies may collect and access would change the volume and handling of customer communications the government can obtain from or through these companies. The effect is indirect and modest.
